1. The animation shows how inflation (US consumer prices, CPI-U) affects a fixed income payment over a 20-year stretch, Aug 2006 to Aug 2026. It uses past data and is labeled "illustrative." The captions tell the viewer to run two checks against a "first check" baseline line. One is a "level check" and the other is a "rising check."

2. A line traces the historical price path across the 20 years. A second gray line then draws out and slides well below the flat "first check" baseline. This gray line is the "level check," which I read as the purchasing power of a payment that stays level. Markers then appear at year 5 and year 20. The captions read "level check: about 9 in 10 by year 5" and "rising check: there after 20 years." A "?" appears at the end. The bar of ten blocks, with the last one dimmed, appears throughout. I'm not sure what it stands for, and I think it may be the "9 in 10."

3. The most likely meaning is that a payment that stays the same loses buying power as prices rise. By year 5 it buys about 90% of what it did at the start, and it keeps falling after that. A payment that rises with prices would, by the 20-year mark, be back at its starting buying power. The "?" suggests the viewer is meant to ask which kind of payout they would want. The image doesn't state the dollar amounts or the exact numbers for the 20-year level case.

4. The animation gives no explicit instruction. A viewer might take away that inflation erodes a flat payout and that a payout which rises over time protects against this. It would also have them weigh that against whatever a rising payout costs, such as a lower starting amount. The cost point is background knowledge about how these products usually work, not something shown in the image. The footer says "US only · history, not a forecast," so past inflation shouldn't be treated as a prediction.

5. The animation did not state this advice. It is my own inference from the level and rising checks and the "?", combined with your annuity context. The animation only presents the comparison and leaves the question open.
